surface_summary: A series of mysterious jewelry thefts occur at Sir James Norris's estate, each marked by a used match left near the missing item. Despite locked doors and difficult access, valuable pieces vanish without disturbance, baffling the police and household. Martin Hewitt investigates and uncovers an unusual accomplice in the thefts.
accepted_facts: Jewelry was stolen from locked rooms with no signs of forced entry
A used match was found near the missing items in each theft
The windows were either open or locked but not tampered with
Vernon Lloyd was present at the estate and had a pet parrot
inferred_conclusions: The thief must have been a human who entered through the window using a ladder
The matches were used to light the room during the thefts
The servants or visitors were responsible for the thefts
mechanism_description: The thefts were carried out by a trained parrot owned by Vernon Lloyd, who was taught to carry a match in its beak and steal jewelry from the dressing-tables. The match was used as a deliberate false clue, placed near the stolen item to mislead investigators. Lloyd acted as the accomplice, releasing the parrot and retrieving the stolen goods without arousing suspicion.
delivery_path: Lloyd places a lit match in the parrot's beak and extinguishes it immediately
The parrot flies to the victim's room through an open or slightly open window
The parrot snatches a single piece of jewelry from the dressing-table
The parrot drops the match near the stolen item to simulate human presence
The parrot returns to Lloyd who collects the stolen jewelry
Lloyd meets the returning party to establish an alibi
The stolen items are disposed of or pawned through accomplices
outcome_result: Vernon Lloyd and his trained parrot are exposed as the culprits behind the mysterious jewelry thefts.

false_assumption.statement: The used matches found near the stolen items were lit and used by a human thief during the robbery.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Matches are commonly used for lighting in dark rooms, so finding a used match near the missing jewelry suggests a human thief used it to see. The police detective also assumed the match indicated the time of the theft.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The match was never lit to provide light but was used as a prop carried by the parrot to mislead investigators about the presence and timing of a human thief.

supporting_points: The ladder was found near the lawn where the gardener worked
The gardener was questioned by the Scotland Yard detective
No stranger was seen near the estate
The gardener had opportunity to access the windows
false_solution.the_one_flaw: The gardener had no motive and was cleared by lack of evidence and alibi

red_herrings.description: A ladder was found lying near the lawn, suggesting it might have been used to access the windows.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The gardener had placed the ladder there earlier in the day for his own work and did not use it for theft.

red_herrings.description: A gas-fitter was working near Mrs. Armitage's door and claimed to have seen no one approach.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The gas-fitter was honest and vigilant, effectively preventing human entry during his watch.

closed_circle.rationale: All persons present at the estate during the thefts were accounted for, and no strangers were seen entering or leaving, forming a closed circle of suspects.

time_windows: few minutes when doors were open
periods when windows were open or propped
trust_channels: Sir James Norris's trust in Lloyd

discriminating_test.design: Martin Hewitt spends a quiet hour alone with the parrot in Lloyd's room, providing it with a match and observing its behavior as it picks up jewelry and drops the match near the item without making noise or disturbance. He compares the marks on the match with the parrot's beak marks and tests the parrot's ability to enter through the window opening.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The parrot can carry the match and jewelry silently and place the match near the stolen item, replicating the crime scene clues.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The parrot successfully performs the theft and match placement without alerting observers or disturbing the room.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed descriptions of the used matches, the locked doors and windows, and the presence of the parrot and its owner. The marks on the match and the parrot's behavior are described clearly, allowing the reader to deduce the role of the trained bird. The improbability of human entry and the pattern of thefts support the solution. No essential clue is withheld.
